verdict.reasoning: Rendered specs/ISO_COBOL.pdf page 49 at 300dpi (E:/Temp/specrecon/v49/spec_p49.png) and read the corresponding markdown span (specs/ISO_COBOL.md lines ~2271-2340). Two independent checks, both against the claim. (1) TEXT CONTENT IS COMPLETE AND VERBATIM. I compared all ten definition entries character-for-character against the printed page. 3.164 source element / 'source unit excluding any contained source units'; 3.165 source unit + its Note 1 to entry; 3.166 standard binary floating-point usages / 'usages float-binary-32, float-binary-64, and float-binary-128'; 3.167 standard decimal floating-point usages / 'usages float-decimal-16 and float-decimal-34'; 3.168 static data; 3.169 subject of the entry; 3.170 subscript (including the quoted value 'ALL'); 3.171 superclass; 3.172 surrogate pair; 3.173 tape drive + its Note 1 to entry. Every term, every definition body, both notes, and the numbering sequence are present and correct. Nothing is missing, added, reworded, or transposed. Not one character of normative text differs. (2) THE FACTUAL OBSERVATION IS ACCURATE BUT IT IS PURE FORMATTING. The PDF page is indeed unruled: it is plain body text from the 'ISO/IEC 1989:2023 (E)' running header to the '(c)ISO/IEC 2023 19' footer, with no horizontal lines. The markdown does carry 12 `---` lines inside the page-49 span (one after the running header, one after each of the ten entries, plus one trailing rule that is the ordinary page-break furniture before ), i.e. 11 rules the PDF does not print. The claim's count and placement are right. But this is exactly the class of difference the verification brief directs me to reject: it is formatting/page furniture, it changes no meaning, and it removes no text. (3) THE STATED HARM RESTS ON A FALSE PREMISE. The claim asserts '`---` is the reserved page-break separator'. I measured the file: it contains 1261 page anchors and only 808 `---` lines. Only 599 of the 1261 page anchors (47%) are preceded by a rule; 655 pages contain NO rule at all, 454 contain exactly one, 137 contain two, and 15 contain three or more. The actual, unambiguous page separator in this transcription is the `` + `## Page N` pair, which is present and correct here. `---` is not reserved for anything, and any consumer that segmented on `---` would already be broken by the 655 ruleless pages and the 137 double-ruled ones - page 49 introduces no new hazard for such a consumer. (4) THE 'TWO-PAGE PATTERN' FRAMING IS ALSO OVERSTATED. Rule counts per page across the whole file: page 49 = 12, page 44 = 12, page 35 = 11, page 36 = 10, pages 31 and 169 = 4, and pages 1, 61, 171, 531, 751, 849, 859, 869, 1229 = 3. So this is a general stylistic habit of the Terms-and-Definitions transcription (short one-line entries get separated), not a two-page defect. The 'only other instance in this batch' hedge may hold for the batch under review, but the pattern claim it is used to support does not. Verdict: the markdown faithfully reproduces every word of PDF page 49. The only difference is decorative thematic breaks, which alter no meaning and threaten no documented convention. real=false.
verdict.corrected_description: Not a content discrepancy. All ten definitions 3.164-3.173 on page 49, including both 'Note 1 to entry' paragraphs, are transcribed completely and verbatim. The markdown does insert 11 decorative `---` thematic breaks that the unruled PDF page does not print (plus 1 legitimate trailing page-break rule, 12 total in the page-49 span) - the observation is factually correct but is formatting only. The claim's rationale is wrong on two counts: `---` is NOT the reserved page-break separator (the separator is `` + `## Page N`; only 599 of 1261 page anchors are preceded by a rule, 655 pages have none, 137 have two), and this is not a two-page pattern (pages 35, 36, 44 and 49 all carry 10-12 rules, with a dozen more pages carrying 3-4) but a general habit of the Terms-and-Definitions transcription. If the extra rules are to be stripped, that is a whole-file cosmetic cleanup, not a page-49 fidelity fix.
